original_question: Can all positive integers be covered by n geometric progressions of integers?
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 31 (On Crittenden and Vanden Eynden's conjecture): "Is it possible to cover all (positive) integers with n geometrical progressions of integers?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right mathematical objects and the right ambient set: it is about covering the positive integers by finitely many geometric progressions whose terms are integers. It is also very close to the paper's wording in Unsolved Problem 31.
missing_details: The paper treats n as fixed: the question is whether, for a given positive integer n, such a finite cover exists.

To be fully stand-alone, one should specify what a geometric progression of integers means here: an infinite sequence determined by a first term a_j and a ratio q_j, as indicated by Comment (a), i.e. a set of the form {a_j q_j^m : m >= 0} with a_j, q_j in N*.
The covering relation should be stated explicitly as a set-theoretic equality: the union of the n progressions is all of N*.
The ambient domain is N*, the positive integers; the paper is not asking about all integers, rationals, or a more general ring.
The first sentence of Unsolved Problem 31 does not impose distinctness of the n geometric progressions; distinctness appears only in the starred follow-up generalization.

The nearby starred sentence is a broader generalization to other classes of positive-integer sequences; your draft does not say whether you mean the solved geometric-progression question itself or that broader open variant. The closest paper-faithful target is the first sentence only.
refined_question: Fix a positive integer n. Do there exist n geometric progressions of positive integers, say G_j = {a_j q_j^m : m >= 0} with a_j, q_j in N* for 1 <= j <= n, whose union is all of N*?
justification: The draft is targeting the first sentence of Unsolved Problem 31 almost verbatim. The surrounding comment identifies the intended parameters of each progression as its first term a_j and ratio q_j, which is the nearby context needed to make the question self-contained. The same comment also shows that the paper immediately gives a negative answer to this exact question by choosing a prime outside the finite set of all listed first terms and ratios. Although the starred continuation asks for a more general necessary-and-sufficient condition for broader classes of sequences, that would broaden your draft beyond the nearest official formulation in the paper.
